title: Read the label, not the rumour
task: Match each thing on the record to what it lets you conclude.
scene: A fire at the freight yard has damaged several unlabelled drums, eighty metres from the river. Three different guesses are already on the radio. Firefighters are choosing what to spray based on whatever you tell them.
assumes: a chemical formula says which elements are in something, and how many of each
takeaway: A name is a label. A formula says what something is made of, which is what decides how it behaves.
why: A formula says which elements are in something and how many of each. That is what decides how it behaves: what it dissolves in, what it reacts with, what it does to water. Change one of those numbers and it is a different substance with different dangers, even though the elements are the same. A trade name carries none of that. It is a word somebody chose, and some of the substances on this list react with water.

scenarios: The formula pairs a metal with a group of atoms carrying a charge.
Two substances have the same elements, in different amounts.
A particle has more electrons than protons.
A label gives a trade name and nothing else.
choices: Probably one of the salts — held together by opposite charges.
Two different substances, not two names for one.
It carries a negative charge overall.
Not enough to say anything about the danger.
rebuttals: A metal with a charged group of atoms is the usual sign of a salt. Two opposite charges holding on to each other.
The same elements in different amounts is a different substance. The amounts are part of what it is.
More electrons than protons means extra negative charge. Counting the two is the whole test.
A trade name with no formula and no strength says nothing about danger. It is a word on a drum.

title: From damaged drum to a first answer
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to happen.
scene: In the mobile laboratory, the first sealed sample from the damaged drums is on the bench. The outside markings are still readable, and there is very little liquid to work with.
assumes: some tests leave a sample as they found it, and some use it up
takeaway: Do the tests that cost nothing before the ones that cannot be taken back.
why: The order is set by what each step costs. The markings on the outside survive only until somebody opens the drum, so they get photographed first, and it costs nothing. Sampling the air above the liquid takes what has already escaped, without opening anything. A test that gives the sample back can be repeated all week if it goes wrong. The test that uses the sample up answers best, and it answers once.

cards: Photograph the markings on the outside, which uses nothing up.
Collect the air above the liquid, without opening the drum.
Take a few drops, and run a test that gives them back.
Spend some of those drops on a test that uses them up.
rebuttals: Photograph first. It costs nothing, and it is the only evidence that stops existing the moment the drum is opened.
The air above the liquid second. It samples what has already got out, without breaching anything.
A test that gives the sample back third. A mistake there costs nothing at all.
The test that uses it up last. It answers best and it answers once, so spend it when you know what to ask.

title: Spend the first of the budget
task: Spend the budget on the evidence that could change the answer.
scene: There is eight hundred pounds left for the first round of tests. Three drums have lost their labels, and the first sample is ready. Firefighters are waiting at the fence for a name.
assumes: two tests that work in different ways can fail in different ways
running the same test twice is not two pieces of evidence
takeaway: Buy the test that could prove you wrong, not the one that makes you look thorough.
question: Which evidence do you buy before telling firefighters what this is?
why: A test result can be precise and still be wrong. Running the same test again shows only that it repeats. Checking the paperwork shows where the sample came from. Quality checks catch particular laboratory mistakes. None of those can say the substance is something else. A test that works by different physics can, which is why it is the one worth buying while there is still a decision hanging on the answer.
answerText: Buy the test that works a different way. It is the only one that could overturn the answer, and everything else only makes the current answer look tidier.

title: How long before it reaches the school
task: Work out how long the cloud takes to reach the school.
scene: A colourless cloud is drifting away from the yard toward two neighbourhoods. Police are holding the evacuation roads open. The wind is steady, and there is a school two kilometres downwind.
assumes: a cloud drifts at roughly the speed of the wind carrying it
takeaway: A hazard has a speed, and a speed turns a distance into the time you have.
question: How long before the cloud reaches the school?
why: A cloud is carried by the wind, so it travels at roughly the wind's speed. Two thousand metres at four metres a second is five hundred seconds, which is a little over eight minutes. That is the whole decision. Eight minutes is enough to move a school if somebody starts now, and not enough if the first thing anybody does is argue. And if the wind picks up, the eight minutes shortens without anybody being told.
answerText: About eight minutes. Two thousand metres at four metres a second is five hundred seconds.

estimate.prompt: The school is 2,000 metres downwind, and the wind is blowing steadily at about 4 metres a second.
estimate.question: How long before the cloud reaches the school?
estimate.explanation: Keep the units together. Metres with metres a second gives seconds. Mixing kilometres in gives an answer a thousand times out.
estimate.solution: 2,000 ÷ 4 is 500 seconds, a little over eight minutes.

title: What changes the cloud
task: Match each change in the field to what it does.
scene: The weather station shows the temperature rising and the pressure falling, with the wind picking up. Crews report vapour pooling in a low channel downwind.
assumes: a gas has a state, and it also has a place, and those change for different reasons
takeaway: Some things change what the gas is doing. Others change where it is going. They are not the same question.
why: Two different things are happening at once. Warming a gas makes it take up more room, and dropping the pressure around it does the same. That is about the gas itself. Whether it hugs the ground or lifts away depends on how heavy it is compared with air, which is a different question again. And where it goes is the wind's business entirely. Nothing about the gas changed when the wind turned. The place it was heading did.

scenarios: The temperature rises, with the pressure much the same.
The pressure falls, with the same gas and the same warmth.
The gas is heavier than air.
The wind shifts while the drum is still leaking.
choices: It takes up more room, in step with the warming.
It takes up more room, because there is less pushing in on it.
It may sink and pool low down, though wind can stir it up.
Where the danger lies has moved, and the map has to move with it.
rebuttals: Warming a gas at the same pressure makes it swell, in step with the warming.
Less pressure pushing in on the same gas lets it swell out. Half the pressure, twice the room.
Being heavier than air decides whether it sinks or lifts, and stirring by the wind can beat it.
A wind shift moves where it goes and changes nothing about the gas itself.

title: Why the drum is worse in the afternoon
task: Say why the same drum reads three times higher.
scene: The same open drum reads three times the vapour at two in the afternoon as it did at six in the morning. Nothing has been added and nothing taken out.
assumes: a liquid is always sending some of itself into the air above it
takeaway: How much of a liquid is in the air above it depends steeply on how warm it is.
question: Same drum, same liquid, three times the vapour. Why?
why: A liquid is always losing molecules into the air above it, and getting some back. How many are up there at once depends on temperature, and it climbs steeply. Ten or fifteen degrees can double it. So the drum that was safe to stand near at dawn is not the same drum at two in the afternoon, with nothing having been added or taken away. It is why measurements get taken at the hottest part of the day.
answerText: It warmed up. A warmer liquid puts far more of itself into the air above it, with nothing else changing at all.

choices: It is warmer, so more of the liquid is in the air above it.
It reacted during the day and made something that evaporates faster.
The morning reading was wrong, because instruments drift when cold.
More evaporated overnight, so what is left is stronger.
rebuttals: Something new would show up as a different substance, and the analysis shows the same one.
Both readings came from the same instrument, and three times over is far more than it can drift.
Evaporating takes away the part that evaporates most easily, which would lower the vapour rather than raise it.

title: Where will it go?
task: Match each kind of chemical to where it ends up.
scene: Runoff from the fire has reached the river. Predict the wrong place and the team samples the wrong thing, and a clean water result gets read by the city as an all-clear.
assumes: some things dissolve in water and some refuse to mix with it
takeaway: Not finding something in the water does not mean it is not in the river.
why: Where a chemical goes follows from what it is like. Some dissolve straight into water and travel with it. Some refuse to mix at all, and sit on top as a film or sink underneath as a layer. And some stick hard to the specks of dirt floating in the water, ride those specks down, and end up in the mud. That last kind is the dangerous case for testing, because the water can come back clean while the river bed holds all of it.

scenarios: Something that dissolves easily in water.
An oily liquid that will not mix with water.
Something that mixes with water the way sugar does.
Something that sticks hard to specks of dirt in the water.
choices: Spread right through the water, travelling with it.
Sits as a separate layer or a film on the surface.
Dissolves well, and moves with the water.
Rides the specks down, and ends up in the mud.
rebuttals: Something that dissolves easily spreads through the water and goes wherever the water goes.
An oily liquid barely mixes at all. It makes its own layer, often a film on top.
Something that mixes the way sugar does dissolves well and travels with the water.
Something that sticks to dirt leaves the water with the dirt, and the dirt settles on the bottom.
columns: What kind of chemical it is

title: Push it back out of the water
task: Work out what eight times the partner chemical does to the metal.
scene: The filtered water holds 3.1 milligrams of dissolved metal in every litre. The limit is 0.5. The rig can put in eight times as much of the partner chemical.
assumes: a dissolved metal and its partner chemical settle at a balance point together
takeaway: Two things that settle together can be pushed apart by adding more of one.
question: Eight times the partner chemical. What happens to the dissolved metal?
why: The metal and its partner are in a tug of war. When there is more of one, less of the other can stay dissolved, and the two move in opposite directions in step. Put in eight times as much partner and the dissolved metal falls to about an eighth. Three point one divided by eight is about 0.39, which is under the limit of half a milligram. A real rig would still have to check that the solid actually settles out and stays out.
answerText: About 0.39 milligrams a litre — an eighth of what it was, which is under the limit.

choices: About 0.39 a litre, because the metal falls by about eight times.
About 3.1 a litre, because dissolving is fixed once a solid is there.
About 24.8 a litre, because both go up together.
About 0.05 a litre, because it falls by eight times eight.
rebuttals: What is fixed is the balance between the two, not the amount of metal. Change one side and the other moves.
The two move in opposite directions. More of one means less of the other, not more of both.
Eight times eight would apply if the two joined up in pairs, and this one joins one for one.

title: Spend the river survey
task: Spend the twenty bottles so the survey can answer all three questions.
scene: The survey has twenty bottles. The chemical barely dissolves, the river runs nine hundred metres from the spill to the water intake, and two samples taken so far disagree six times over.
assumes: different places and different parts of a river answer different questions
a clean water sample cannot rule out a chemical sitting in the mud
takeaway: A sampling plan is the set of questions it can answer, and every bottle spent is a question given up.
question: How do you spend twenty bottles without leaving a question unanswered?
why: Three questions need answering and each needs its own bottles. What is reaching the intake now, which is what the city acts on today. What the river looked like before the spill, which is the only way to know whether a reading is unusual. And whether the chemical has left the water for the mud, which is where this kind goes. A pretty stained bank is interesting and answers none of the three. Twenty bottles cannot buy everything.
answerText: Spend most of them on the intake over time, on upstream water, and on the mud and the specks in the water. The stained bank is what to give up.

title: Undo the dilution
task: Work out what was really in the river sample.
scene: The laboratory watered the sample down before measuring it. So the instrument reports what was in the vial, and the city is about to compare that number with a limit.
assumes: watering a sample down lowers the reading by a known amount
takeaway: What was done to a sample before it was measured is part of the answer.
question: What was really in the river sample?
why: Samples get watered down so the reading lands inside the range the instrument can measure. That has to be undone before the number means anything about the river. Ten millilitres made up to a hundred is ten times weaker, so the river figure is ten times the reading. Report the reading as it stands and the river looks ten times cleaner than it is. Nothing about the number would show that anything was wrong.
answerText: Twenty-five milligrams a litre. The reading was 2.5, and the sample had been watered down ten times.

estimate.prompt: Ten millilitres of river water were made up to a hundred millilitres. The instrument then read 2.5 milligrams a litre.
estimate.question: What was really in the river sample?
estimate.relationship: River figure = the reading × the final volume ÷ the sample taken.
estimate.explanation: Ten times weaker means the answer is ten times the reading. Report the reading as it stands and the river looks ten times cleaner than it is.
labels: 100 mL (what it was made up to)
10 mL (how much river water was used)
0.25 mg/L (the smallest the instrument can see)

title: Say what should happen, then check
task: Predict what watering it down does, do it, and check the reading.
scene: The instrument gives a number for anything you put in front of it, whether or not the number means anything. This reading sits above the range it was set up for.
assumes: the reading goes up in step with how much is in the sample
watering something down by half halves what is in it
takeaway: Predict what a change should do, make it, and check. That is what turns a reading into a result.
question: What should the reading become after watering it down, and does the rerun agree?
why: Above the range it was set up for, an instrument still prints a number, and nobody knows what it means. Watering the sample down by half should halve the reading, and that is a prediction worth making before doing it. A reading of 1.34 should become about 0.67. The rerun gives 0.68, which is inside the trusted range and agrees with the prediction. Then the answer can be doubled back, and both halves of it have been checked.
answerText: Predict about 0.67, water it down by half, and rerun. The 0.68 that comes back agrees, so doubling it back gives an answer worth reporting.

title: Map the river with thirty samples
task: Say where the samples should go.
scene: The city wants a picture of eleven kilometres of river. The laboratory can run thirty samples. The field kit is far rougher than the laboratory.
assumes: a map is worth whatever the decisions made from it are worth
takeaway: Good numbers in the wrong places and rough numbers in the right ones both mislead.
question: You cannot sample every metre. Where do the samples go?
why: There are two ways to waste this. Perfect chemistry at points nobody cares about, or lots of samples with a kit whose numbers nobody trusts. Both give a confident map that misleads. Every decision the city makes happens at the water intake, so that is where the detail belongs. Sampling where the water looks stained samples the staining, and this chemical has no colour.
answerText: Thickly round the drinking water intake. That is where every decision gets made, and detail anywhere else is detail nobody acts on.

choices: Thickly, round the drinking water intake.
Spread along the river, above and below, over several days.
Into repeats and checks at the places already planned.
Wherever the water looks stained.
rebuttals: Spreading along the river shows where it is going, and it is the second question rather than the first.
Repeats and checks make each number trustworthy and place none of them. That is how you sample, not where.
Sampling the stained water samples the staining. This chemical has no colour at all.

title: How much heat is stored in there
task: Work out how much energy the bath has taken in.
scene: The visible fire has been out for two hours, and the water bath beside the damaged bay is still warming. Fire Command wants the size of the heat before deciding whether the cooling on site is enough.
assumes: different materials need different amounts of energy to warm by one degree
takeaway: A small temperature rise across something heavy is a very large amount of energy.
question: How much energy has the bath taken in?
why: Warming something by one degree takes energy, and how much depends on what it is and how much of it there is. Water is stubborn: every kilogram needs 4.2 units for each degree. Two thousand kilograms warming five degrees is forty-two thousand of them. Five degrees sounds like nothing, and against that much water it is an enormous amount of energy arriving from somewhere. That is what makes the small number worth calculating.
answerText: About forty-two thousand units of heat. Five degrees sounds like nothing until it is multiplied by two thousand kilograms.

estimate.prompt: The bath holds 2,000 kilograms of water. Every kilogram takes 4.2 units of heat for each degree, and it has warmed by 5 degrees.
estimate.question: How much energy has the bath taken in?
estimate.relationship: Heat taken in = how much there is × what one degree costs × how many degrees.
estimate.explanation: Five degrees is the temperature change, not the temperature. Using 300 instead would answer a question about heating it from nothing, which is not what happened.
labels: 4.2 units for each kilogram, each degree
2,260 units for each kilogram (boiling it away)

title: Left-over heat, or something still going?
task: Say which explanation fits both bays.
scene: Two bays saw the same fire. Ninety minutes after the cooling stopped, the east bay is cooling and the west bay is warming. The west bay is giving off more gas, and the hot spot has not moved.
assumes: heat flows from hot to cold, and never the other way by itself
takeaway: Something that keeps getting hotter after the fire is out is making its own heat.
question: Is this heat left over, or something still running?
why: Left-over heat can only drain away once the fire is out. That is what the east bay is doing, and it is the control. The west bay is doing the opposite: rising, with more gas coming off, and the hot spot sitting in one place at the drum stack. Nothing that is merely cooling behaves like that. Something in there is making heat. And a bad sensor would push both bays the same way, which is exactly why two bays are worth having.
answerText: Something is still running in the west bay. Left-over heat drains away, which is what the east bay is doing.

choices: Something is still reacting in the west bay, and making heat.
Heat left over from the fire is still draining away.
The temperature sensors are wrong.
Warm liquid is circulating and carrying heat over there.
Nothing odd. Two bays never cool at the same rate.
choiceMechanisms: It gets hotter after the fire is out, more gas comes off, and the hot spot stays put. That is heat being made.
Something heavy takes hours to give back the heat it soaked up.
All four sensors share one reference, so one bad reference would spoil them all.
Moving liquid carries a hot patch about, and one sensor can catch it.
Two bays that saw the same fire will cool at different speeds.
rebuttals: Left-over heat is exactly what the east bay is doing, which is why the east bay is the control. It cannot rise after the fire goes out.
One shared reference is a real worry and it would move both bays the same way. West rises while east falls.
Moving liquid carries a hot patch around. This hot spot has not moved at all.
Two bays cooling at different speeds is ordinary. One heating while the other cools is not.
text.headline: Ninety minutes after the cooling stopped, the west bay is still climbing.

title: Control the self-heating
task: Say what has to be in place before the site is released.
scene: Fire Command wants the site released tonight. Bay three has gone from thirty-one degrees to forty-four in eight hours, and it is climbing faster than it was. There are four tonnes in there.
assumes: a trend says something a single reading cannot
takeaway: A site is safe to leave when somebody can watch the trend, not when one reading looks fine.
question: Fire Command wants it released tonight. What do you require first?
why: Self-heating is a race. Something inside is making heat, and the surroundings are carrying heat away, and only the trend says which is winning. One reading cannot. So the thing to insist on is watching it continuously, because that is what turns a guess into a warning. Working out the chemistry takes days and is worth starting. Bringing cooling in changes the race and needs to know which way it is running first.
answerText: Continuous watching of the temperature. It is the only thing that says which way the race is going, and it can be in place tonight.

choices: Watch the temperature and the heat continuously, in every bay.
Take material away and test how much heat it makes.
Bring cooling on site, and prove it works if the supply fails.
One more reading at the door as the crews leave.
rebuttals: Testing the material gives the mechanism and the rate, and it takes days. Start it, and it does not decide tonight.
Cooling changes the race, and it has to know which way the race is running before it can be sized.
One reading at the door is exactly the measurement that failed this afternoon. One bay was warm and falling. One was warm and rising.

title: How much more acidic
task: Work out how many times more acidic the water is.
scene: The intake water reads four on the acid scale. Ordinary water reads seven. The plant is about to add something to bring it back, and wants the size of the problem first.
assumes: each step down the acid scale means ten times more acid
takeaway: A scale where each step is ten times hides how big a difference really is.
question: How many times more acidic is the intake water than ordinary water?
why: The acid scale is not like a ruler. Each step down means ten times more acid, not one more unit of it. So four is not a little below seven. It is three steps, and three steps is ten times ten times ten. A thousand times more acid than ordinary water. That is why a number that looks like a small change on paper needs a great deal more neutralising than anybody expects.
answerText: A thousand times. Three steps down the scale, and each step is ten times more.

estimate.prompt: The intake reads 4 and ordinary water reads 7. Each step down the scale means ten times more acid.
estimate.question: How many times more acidic is the intake water?
estimate.relationship: Times more acidic = ten, multiplied by itself once for every step.
estimate.explanation: Three steps is ten times ten times ten. Subtracting instead gives three, which is the number of steps rather than the answer.

title: Why the first dose overshot
task: Say what the test explains about the overshoot.
scene: A dose worked out from the intake reading overshot badly. The bench test is now up beside a reference curve for a simple acid, with fresh checks on the meter from the same electrode.
assumes: some acids hold most of their acid back, and let it out as you neutralise
takeaway: A reading tells you what is loose right now. It does not tell you what is held in reserve.
question: Which explanation accounts for the flat stretch and the dose it really took?
why: The reading measures the acid that is loose in the water at that moment. Some acids hold most of theirs back, and release more every time you neutralise what is loose. So the reading looks mild while the amount actually needed is five times bigger. That is what the long flat stretch on the test is: base going in and the reading barely moving, because more acid keeps arriving from the reserve.
answerText: The water holds a reserve of acid that the reading cannot see. It lets more out as you neutralise, which is why the dose was five times bigger.

choices: The water holds a reserve of acid that the reading cannot see.
It is a simple acid, and the reading is what it says.
The meter is out of adjustment.
The stuff being added is stronger than the label says.
Nothing odd. Treatment always needs extra.
choiceMechanisms: A long flat stretch and a dose five times bigger is what a hidden reserve does.
Read it, work out the acid, and add the matching amount.
A drifting meter would explain why the sum came out wrong.
Something stronger than labelled would overshoot whatever the water was like.
Operators routinely add extra to be sure.
rebuttals: A simple acid is the reference curve, on the same axes. It finishes early and sharply, and this one does neither.
The meter was checked against two known liquids and it was right. It is answering a different question from the one the dose needed.
Something over-strength would overshoot and it would also finish sooner. This took five times more, not less.
Adding extra is a habit, not an explanation. It cannot produce a flat stretch or a five-fold demand.
text.headline: The intake reads mildly acidic. A dose worked out from that reading overshoots badly.

title: Neutralise without overshooting
task: Set the slow-down and stop rules before the stream runs.
scene: The pump is primed and the operators are waiting on the valve. The water is acidic and the iron pipe is corroding. Every change to the pump shows up one reading later.
assumes: the meter shows what the pump did one reading ago, not what it is doing now
each step on the acid scale is ten times, so equal steps are not equal amounts
takeaway: When the answer arrives late, the rule has to fire early.
question: Where do the two thresholds go, when every change shows up a reading late?
why: The pump acts now and the meter shows it later. So waiting until the meter reads what you want guarantees going past it, because more base is already on its way through the tank. Writing the rules first is what stops that. Slow the feed while the water can still absorb it, and stop it early enough that what is already in the pipe carries the reading the rest of the way. The threshold is a decision, not a description.
answerText: Slow the feed near 5.8 and stop it near 6.5. Each change shows up a reading later, so waiting for the number you want arrives too late.

title: Where the metal is going
task: Match each thing happening at the metal to its part in the circuit.
scene: Acidic water is flowing through a section where two different metals are bolted together. An inspection has found one small break in the coating. The team wants the circuit understood before choosing a repair.
assumes: rusting is electricity, moving in a loop, with metal as one of the ingredients
takeaway: Rusting is a loop. Break any part of the loop and it stops.
why: Rusting is not simply metal going bad. It is a circuit with four parts: a place losing metal, a place taking the electrons, a path through the metal, and a path through the water. Two different metals bolted together in water provide all four at once. And a coating with one small hole is worse than no coating, because everything that would have been spread over the whole pipe now goes through that one spot.

scenarios: Metal is dissolving away into the water.
A surface is taking in the electrons that were left behind.
Two different metals are bolted together, in water.
A coating has one small break in it.
choices: This is where the metal is actually being lost.
The other half of the loop, which loses no metal.
Everything the loop needs, in one place.
The whole attack, squeezed into one small spot.
rebuttals: Metal dissolving away is where the loss happens. That is the end of the loop that eats the pipe.
A surface taking the electrons is the other half. It completes the loop and loses nothing itself.
Two different metals in water give a place to lose metal, a place to take electrons, and both paths at once.
One hole in a coating forces the whole attack through one small area, which is why it goes through fast.
columns: What is happening at the metal
Which part of the loop that is

title: How fast is the wall going
task: Work out how deep the loss is each year.
scene: A test piece from the intake has lost two kilograms of steel in a year, spread over four square metres. The wall that is left is six millimetres thick.
assumes: a rate only becomes a decision when it is compared with a thickness
takeaway: An amount lost is not a warning until somebody turns it into a depth.
question: How much depth is being lost each year?
why: Two kilograms a year sounds alarming and means nothing alone. Spread over four square metres of steel, it works out at about six hundredths of a millimetre a year. At that rate a six millimetre wall lasts most of a century. That is the useful answer, and it is also a warning about averages. The same two kilograms at one hole goes through in a season.
answerText: About 0.06 millimetres a year, spread evenly. At that rate the wall lasts most of a century — if it really is spread evenly.

estimate.prompt: The pipe loses about 2.0 kilograms of steel a year over 4.0 square metres. Steel weighs 7,900 kilograms for every cubic metre.
estimate.question: How much depth is being lost each year?
estimate.relationship: Depth each year = the weight lost ÷ (how heavy the steel is × the area).
estimate.explanation: Divide by the density of the metal, not of water. The two differ by nearly eight times, and only one of them is the pipe.
estimate.solution: 2.0 ÷ (7,900 × 4.0) is about 0.000063 metres, which is 0.063 millimetres a year.

title: Protect the pipe
task: Say which control goes in first.
scene: The thinnest part of the intake pipe has three millimetres of wall left, and the loss has sped up eight times. The gallery stays cleared until the first control is chosen. Water is still flowing.
assumes: a loop stops when any one part of it is broken
takeaway: Break the loop where you can break it today, and do the rest afterwards.
question: Which fix breaks the problem most directly?
why: The loop needs four parts, and breaking any one stops it. The water is acidic, which makes one path easy. The two metals bolted together supply the other. Separating those metals cuts the loop, and it can be done today. Changing the water works and is tangled up with everything else the plant has to do. A new coating helps, and it concentrates the attack wherever it fails.
answerText: Separate the two metals where they are bolted together. That breaks the loop directly, and everything else can follow.

choices: Separate the two metals where they are bolted together.
Change the water so it is less aggressive.
Recoat the pipe, and inspect the coating for holes.
Reissue the leak report with the photographs attached.
rebuttals: Changing the water works, and it is tangled up with everything else the treatment has to do, including the neutralising that started this.
A coating blocks one path, and it sends the whole attack through any hole it later gets. That needs inspections with it.
A better-looking report changes nothing in the loop, and it is the intake that is at risk.

title: What did the treatment actually do?
task: Close the ledger, and find what the water figure does not account for.
scene: The pilot treated a batch holding a hundred kilograms of the chemical. The treated water, the sludge and the gas coming off have each been measured. The city is waiting to hear whether it was destroyed.
assumes: nothing simply disappears; it ends up somewhere
water getting cleaner does not say where the chemical went
takeaway: Taking something out of one place is not destroying it. The ledger has to close.
question: How much is missing from the measured streams, and does that support destroying it?
why: A hundred kilograms went in, and six are left in the water. That is not ninety-four destroyed. Seventy-one are in the sludge and three went off as gas, which is eighty accounted for. Twenty are missing, and the bench has already seen something new that nobody has measured. So the honest sentence is that the treatment moved most of it and changed some of it. Destroyed is a different claim, and this ledger does not support it.
answerText: Eighty kilograms are accounted for, so twenty are missing. Until somebody finds those, this is moving it about rather than destroying it.

title: Put the treatment in order
task: Put the four stages in the order they have to run.
scene: Four stages are on the table and the plant wants an order for them. Riverton has one intake, and it cannot run this experiment twice while the water is off.
assumes: a filter can only take out something that is already solid
takeaway: Each stage is ordered by what it leaves the next one to work with.
why: Each stage hands something to the next. The first changes the metal into a form that can turn solid, because nothing later can make a solid out of something that will not make one. Changing the water then actually turns it solid. Only then is there anything for a filter to catch: filtering dissolved metal removes nothing at all. And the carbon goes last, because sending solids into a carbon bed clogs it within hours.

cards: Change the dissolved metal into the form that can turn solid.
Change the water, so that form actually turns solid.
Let it settle, and filter the solid out.
Polish what is left on carbon, for whatever stayed dissolved.
rebuttals: Changing the form first. Nothing later can make a solid out of something that will not make one.
Changing the water second. This is the step that actually produces the solid.
Settling and filtering third, once there is a solid to catch. Filtering dissolved metal catches nothing.
Carbon last. Send solids into a carbon bed and it clogs within hours, and everything after it stops.

title: Choose what the pilot measures
task: Say what the pilot has to measure.
scene: The pilot has room for one question, four weeks, and a tenth of the flow. All three methods claim to remove the chemical, and the full plant is committed in June whatever the pilot finds.
assumes: something that removes a chemical has to put it somewhere
takeaway: Measure the thing that would tell the options apart, not the thing they all agree on.
question: All three remove it. What does the pilot have to measure?
why: Every method here removes the chemical. That is why they are all on the table, and it is why measuring removal cannot choose between them. What separates them is what they leave behind: what the chemical turns into, and where the waste ends up. A pilot that measures only the target will pick whichever method makes the most new problem fastest, and it will look like a triumph while it does it.
answerText: What the chemical turns into. Every method removes it, so removal cannot tell them apart, and what they leave behind can.

choices: What the chemical turns into, and how harmful those things are.
How much of the chemical each method removes, in real river water.
Whether the material wears out, and where the used waste goes.
The highest removal anybody can reach, at any dose.
rebuttals: Comparing removal is the comparison, and judged on that alone it picks whichever method makes the most byproduct fastest.
Whether it wears out and where the waste goes both matter, and they come once a method is chosen. They describe the life of a decision already made.
Chasing the highest removal at any dose is exactly the narrow aim that produced a sludge with twenty kilograms missing from it.

title: Two candidates, one difference
task: Say what settles which of the two it is.
scene: Two substances fit the result equally well, and their formulas differ by a single oxygen. There is an instrument here that weighs molecules, and it has already measured this sample.
assumes: what a molecule is made of decides what it weighs
takeaway: When two answers fit, use a measurement that depends on something they differ in.
question: Two candidates, differing by one oxygen. What settles it?
why: The two fit the first test equally well, so nothing about that test can choose. What they do differ in is weight: one oxygen atom is sixteen units, and there is an instrument here that weighs molecules directly. Sixteen units is an enormous difference to that instrument. The order things come out in follows chemistry rather than weight, and how big the peak is follows how much there is. Neither says which substance it is.
answerText: Weigh them. One oxygen is sixteen units, which is far more than the instrument that weighs molecules can miss.

choices: The weight of the molecule, which differs by sixteen between them.
The order it came out in, since the heavier one always comes later.
How big the peak is, since the heavier one gives more signal.
Neither, because they are the same kind of substance.
rebuttals: What comes out first follows chemistry rather than weight. Heavier things sometimes come out earlier.
How big a peak is depends on how much there is, and on the substance. It says nothing about which one.
Sixteen units apart is easy for an instrument that weighs molecules. That is exactly the tie it is built to break.

title: Close the gaps before release
task: Match each weakness in the evidence to what would close it.
scene: A number can be perfectly correct and still answer the wrong question. The pipes are about to be brought back up to pressure on the strength of this evidence.
assumes: a sample tells you about the place and the moment it was taken
takeaway: A correct number is only useful if the sample it came from matches the decision.
why: Each of these is a different kind of gap and none of the fixes swaps for another. Sampling only where the water leaves the plant misses the taps people drink from. Sampling after running the tap for ages measures water nobody receives. An instrument that cannot see below the limit cannot test the limit. And one laboratory that both fixed the water and checked the water has marked its own homework, which no amount of good chemistry corrects.

scenarios: Only the water leaving the plant was sampled.
Samples were taken after running the tap for a long time.
The instrument cannot see anything below the limit.
One laboratory both fixed the water and checked it.
choices: Sample at the taps people actually drink from.
Write down the running, and sample the way people really use it.
Use an instrument that can see below the limit.
Get somebody independent to check it.
rebuttals: Sampling where the water leaves the plant misses the taps where people drink. Sample where the exposure happens.
Water sampled after a long run is water nobody receives. Record the running, and sample realistically.
An instrument that cannot see below the limit cannot test the limit at all. That needs a better instrument.
One laboratory doing both jobs has marked its own homework. That gap closes with an independent check.

title: Open, hold, or open with conditions
task: Move and narrow the band, and say whether the valves can open.
scene: The pumps are idle while the board meets. The result is nine against a limit of ten, give or take two. Operators are waiting at the valves, and the city has already been given two different reopening times.
assumes: the band shown is the doubt that this decision has to live with
a middle below a limit is not a pass if the band crosses it
takeaway: Moving the middle and narrowing the band are different moves, and a boundary needs both.
question: Can the whole band be brought under the limit, or only its middle?
why: Nine against a limit of ten looks like a pass until the band is drawn. Give or take two means the honest range runs up to eleven, and eleven is over. A rerun can move the middle without proving the band was too wide. Better sampling can narrow the band without moving the middle. Neither alone gets the top of the band under ten. Both together give 8.6 with a band of one, and a top edge of 9.6.
answerText: Neither move is enough alone. Do both, and the band becomes 8.6 give or take one, with its top edge at 9.6.

title: What each claim has earned
task: Match each state of the evidence to what should be done with it.
scene: The city wants one sentence, and the chemistry does not support one. Turning all of it into a single green light is how a place gets reopened above a problem nobody wrote down.
assumes: evidence comes in strengths, and a claim is only as strong as the weakest step under it
takeaway: Readiness is claim by claim. There is no single green light.
why: At the end of this, the evidence sits in four states, and each needs a different sentence. Something confirmed two separate ways can be written down as settled. Something likely, with no way to measure it yet, is provisional, and saying so keeps the record honest. Clean water above dirty mud is being managed rather than solved. And corrosion held inside a narrow window is a condition.

scenarios: Confirmed by two separate methods, with checks.
Likely, and there is no way to measure it yet.
The water passes, and the mud is still contaminated.
Corrosion is under control while the water chemistry holds.
choices: Write it down as settled, with the methods.
Call it provisional, and keep working on how to measure it.
Keep managing the mud, and keep watching for it coming back.
Keep going under conditions, with triggers written down.
rebuttals: Confirmed two ways with checks is the strongest claim here. Write down the methods and treat it as settled.
Something likely with no way to measure it cannot be quantified yet. Say so, and keep developing the method.
Clean water over dirty mud is a managed situation rather than a solved one, and the managing is what has to continue.
Corrosion held inside a narrow window is conditional. The condition needs triggers, or it is just a hope.

title: Did the cell do what it should?
task: Compare what the cell removed with what it should have removed.
scene: The polishing cell ran for six hours. From the current it drew, it should have taken out about four and a half kilograms of metal. The water figures say it took out three and a half.
assumes: the electricity a cell uses sets the most metal it could possibly remove
takeaway: Comparing what happened with what should have happened is how a claim gets checked.
question: What share of the possible removal did the cell actually manage?
why: The electricity going into a cell sets a ceiling. It cannot take out more metal than the current allows, however good it is. So the check is simple: what it actually removed, against what it could have. Three and a half out of four and a half is about eighty per cent, which is a real cell doing well. A figure over a hundred would mean the water measurements are wrong, or somebody has mixed up which tank they came from.
answerText: About 80 per cent of what the electricity allowed. Anything over a hundred would mean a measurement was wrong.

estimate.prompt: The current the cell drew allows at most 4.5 kilograms of metal to be removed. The water figures say 3.6 kilograms came out.
estimate.question: What share of the possible removal did the cell manage?
estimate.relationship: Share = what it removed ÷ what it could have removed × 100.
estimate.explanation: Divide the actual by the possible, not the other way round. Upside down gives 125 per cent, which would be a cell removing more metal than the electricity allows.
estimate.solution: 3.6 ÷ 4.5, times a hundred, is 80 per cent.

title: What the city keeps
task: Say what the city should keep paying for.
scene: The temporary laboratory is being packed up as the emergency money ends. The plant is running. The mud still holds about seventy-one kilograms, and one monitoring station has funding after next month.
assumes: falling below a limit is not the same as being gone
takeaway: What outlasts an emergency is the part that went quiet, not the part that stopped.
question: The emergency money is about to move elsewhere. What does the city keep?
why: Nothing here was destroyed. Seventy-one kilograms are in the mud, twenty were never accounted for, and something new is still being worked out. All of it is below a limit rather than gone. Watching the water, the mud and the air is the only thing on this list that would notice any of it coming back. Corrosion control protects the pipes, which is a different problem. Keeping the records costs almost nothing and should happen anyway.
answerText: Keep the monitoring, across water, mud and air. It is the only thing that would notice any of this coming back.

choices: Long-term monitoring of the water, the mud and the air.
Corrosion control, and making the plant more robust.
Open records, reference samples and written methods.
Nothing. The records can close once the review is out.
rebuttals: Corrosion control protects the pipes, and the pipes are a different hazard from the seventy-one kilograms in the mud.
Open records and reference samples preserve the method, cost very little, and should happen whatever this budget does.
Closing the records destroys the only account of how any of it was measured, and the next city starts from nothing.
